knownFor: Teacher and Bible scholar at Alexandria and Caesarea, who wrote commentaries on Scripture and a book of doctrine that was argued over for centuries.
shortDescription: Origen taught the Christian faith at Alexandria, in Egypt, and then at Caesarea, in Palestine, and spent his life asking what Scripture means beneath its plain words. He set the Hebrew text beside the Greek translations, and was tortured under the emperor Decius.
datesNote: No old source used here gives a calendar year for his life. Eusebius sets the persecution in which his father died in the tenth year of the emperor Severus, when Origen was not quite seventeen. He sets the move to Caesarea in the tenth year of the emperor Alexander. He says Origen was tortured under Decius and died in the time of Gallus, aged sixty-nine. The years in the translators' notes are their own reckoning, and the third century comes from the modern dating of those reigns.
placeNote: Alexandria, in Egypt, where he grew up and first taught; Caesarea, on the coast of Palestine, where he was ordained and later settled and taught; Tyre, where Jerome says he died and was buried

keyWorks.title: On First Principles
keyWorks.about: his teaching on God, Christ, souls and how Scripture is to be read. Eusebius lists it among the works he wrote at Alexandria. Most of it is read in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin, and Rufinus says he left out or reworded what he found on the Trinity that disagreed with Origen's teaching elsewhere. The part on reading Scripture also survives in Origen's Greek, kept in the Philocalia

keyWorks.title: Against Celsus
keyWorks.about: eight books answering True Discourse, which Celsus the Epicurean had written against the Christians. Eusebius says he wrote them when he was over sixty

keyWorks.title: The Hexapla
keyWorks.about: the Hebrew text set beside the Greek translations; the church historian Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen left us copies of it. Jerome says Origen searched out three more translations, which Jerome himself had from Origen's library

traces: Eusebius of Caesarea tells of two brothers, Gregory and Athenodorus, who came to Origen at Caesarea full of zeal for Greek and Roman learning. He gave them a love of philosophy and turned them to the study of divinity. After five years with him, both became bishops in Pontus.

Jerome says Gregory gave a speech of thanks to Origen before a large gathering, with Origen present. The speech says Origen had his pupils read all the philosophers and poets, rejecting none but those who deny God and providence.
A letter from Origen to a Gregory he calls his son survives in the Philocalia. It urges him to take from Greek philosophy what can prepare for Christianity, as geometry and grammar serve philosophy.
Dionysius, one of his pupils, took charge of the teaching at Alexandria after Heraclas and later became bishop there, Eusebius says.

Pamphilus of Caesarea collected a library of his works and copied most of them by hand, and Jerome says they were still kept in the library at Caesarea. Eusebius gathered as many of his letters as he could find and arranged them in books.

Pamphilus, with Eusebius, wrote a Defense of Origen. Photius says it was in six books, five written by Pamphilus in prison and the sixth by Eusebius after Pamphilus's death. Its first book answers his accusers from Origen's own words, above all on On First Principles, the books they said differed most from the church's teaching.
Athanasius of Alexandria, defending the Council of Nicaea, called on Origen as a hardworking witness that the Word of God always existed with the Father.

The church historian Socrates says Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus got Origen's books and drew from them the right reading of Scripture. When the Arians, who taught that the Son of God had a beginning, quoted Origen, the two showed that the Arians did not understand him.
Gregory of Nazianzus, sending the Philocalia to a friend, called it a selection of passages useful to students of literature.

Jerome, attacked because his new Latin translation of the Old Testament seemed to censure the Seventy, the old Greek translation, answered that Origen himself had marked where the Seventy fell short of the Hebrew.
remembered: Porphyry, a pagan philosopher who met Origen when Porphyry was young and later wrote against the Christians, said Origen took the Greeks' figurative way of explaining their mystery rites and applied it to the Jewish scriptures. Eusebius says Porphyry spoke truly of his hard work and learning.

Methodius of Olympus wrote On the Resurrection against him. By Photius's extracts, Methodius charged that Origen taught the body was given to the soul as a fetter after the fall, and that the soul had lived without a body before.

The church historian Socrates of Constantinople, who defended Origen, names four men who attacked him: Methodius of Olympus, Eustathius of Antioch, Apollinaris and Theophilus of Alexandria. He says each blamed a different point, and none charged Origen with unsound teaching on the Trinity.
Socrates of Constantinople also says Theophilus of Alexandria wrote to the bishops condemning Origen's books, to hide his real aim, which was to move against John Chrysostom.
Epiphanius of Cyprus charged, and Jerome repeated, that Origen taught even the devil would one day repent.

Epiphanius wrote against Origen more than a century after his death. He says that in Alexandria Origen was made to put incense on an altar fire and was cast out by the confessors and the church. Unable to bear the mockery, Epiphanius adds, he left for Palestine.
About three centuries after his death, a council at Constantinople named Origen in its eleventh anathema, a formal curse, beside Arius and others, with their impious writings.

The church historian Evagrius Scholasticus says that monks petitioned the council against Origen's teachings. He says the council sent the emperor Justinian a report after crying out against Origen and those who shared his errors, and attached chapters setting out what Origen's followers had been taught to hold.
The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, a much later Egyptian chronicle, says Demetrius cut him off for writing unlawful books of magic, and that he then wrote treatises full of blasphemies.

uncertain: The witnesses. Most of his life rests on Eusebius of Caesarea, who wrote about two generations after his death, from letters and from people who knew him. Eusebius was a defender: he says he and Pamphilus wrote their Defense of Origen because of faultfinders. Jerome wrote over a century after Origen's death, and Photius, who summarizes Pamphilus's lost account, about six centuries after.

Jerome says Origen was ordained in Palestine on a journey, which so enraged his bishop Demetrius that he wrote everywhere to ruin Origen's name. Eusebius of Caesarea orders it differently: Demetrius wrote against Origen first, seeing him prosper, and the ordination came after.

Photius, summarizing Pamphilus, says Origen was ordained against the church's rule, as he was leaving for Athens without his bishop's permission. A gathering of bishops and some presbyters then ruled that he must not live or teach in Alexandria but could keep his priesthood, and later Demetrius and some Egyptian bishops took his priesthood from him too. No earlier source used here tells of this gathering. Jerome says Origen made the journey with a church letter.

Eusebius of Caesarea is our witness that Origen took a saying of Jesus too literally and made himself a eunuch. He adds that Demetrius at first admired the act, then wrote of it to bishops everywhere as most foolish. Jerome says only that Demetrius was wildly enraged at Origen after his ordination.

In his Commentary on Matthew, Origen writes that some took the saying on eunuchs in a bodily sense and did it to themselves, out of fear of God but without understanding, and brought reproach on themselves. He names no one, himself included.
In his Commentary on John, Origen says he came out of the storm in Alexandria and that an enemy attacked him in new writings. He does not say who the enemy was.

Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen died in the time of the emperor Gallus, at sixty-nine. Jerome adds that he died at Tyre and was buried there. Photius says Pamphilus and others wrote that he died a martyr at Caesarea under Decius. Photius himself thinks the account of Tyre truer, unless the letters Origen is said to have written after the persecution are forged.

We read On First Principles mostly in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin. Rufinus says in his preface that wherever he found anything on the Trinity contrary to what Origen taught elsewhere, he left it out or set it down in words that agree with the rule of faith. Jerome, who made his own translation, says Rufinus cut out what gave offense, while he himself set the books down just as they stood in the Greek.

The simple believers. In On First Principles, the third group who go wrong about God are, in Crombie's English, the simpler among those who profess to belong to the church. In Lewis's English, they are the less sophisticated among those who have left the church.
He does not say every passage has three senses. He writes that some passages have no bodily, plain sense at all, and that the plain sense alone helps a great many simple believers.

Where the way of reading came from. Origen points to Paul, who said the story of Hagar and Sarah contains an allegory. Porphyry says Origen learned it from Greek writers. Porphyry also said Origen had been raised a pagan Greek and went over to the Christians; Eusebius calls this false, since his parents taught him Christ.
Whether Origen's name stood in the council's eleventh anathema from the first is a question raised by modern scholars, not by the old sources used here.

The quotations. Origen's Greek of On First Principles and of Book VI of his Commentary on John is not held, so their modern English follows the printed English translations. Porphyry's Greek is held only in a damaged scan, so the English printed with his words is McGiffert's.

timeline.when: In the tenth year of the emperor Severus
timeline.headline: A boyhood in Scripture, and his father's death
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, from letters and from people who knew him

lines.when: In the tenth year of Severus
lines.text: Under the emperor Severus, believers are brought to Alexandria from all Egypt to be tried. Origen's father is among them, and is beheaded while his son is still young.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.1 and VI.2.2; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 32397-32460, 32523-32533

lines.text: His father has him learn and recite Scripture every day, before any Greek studies.

The boy is not content with the plain, obvious meaning and keeps asking what the inspired words truly mean. His father rebukes him to his face, for appearance's sake, not to search past his age or past the plain meaning, but thanks God for him in private.
They say his father often stood by the sleeping boy, uncovered his chest as if the Spirit of God dwelt within it, and kissed it.
lines.note: Eusebius gives this as what is said, not as what he knew.

lines.when: In the tenth year of Severus
lines.text: When his father is arrested, the boy longs to die a martyr too. His mother begs him to stay, then hides all his clothes so he cannot go out.

lines.when: In the tenth year of Severus
lines.text: He writes to his father in prison, urging him not to change his mind for the family's sake.

lines.when: In the tenth year of Severus
lines.text: His father dies a martyr. Origen, not quite seventeen, is left with his mother and six younger brothers, and the family's property is seized.
He earns his living by teaching grammar and literature.
With the teachers of the faith driven away by persecution, some pagans come to him to hear the word of God, and he takes charge of the teaching.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.3.1 and 3; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 32670-32674, 32732-32733
lines.note: Eusebius says Origen tells this himself.

lines.text: He goes with martyrs to their deaths and greets them with a kiss, so that crowds nearly attack him, and soldiers are posted around his house.

Demetrius, the bishop of Alexandria, entrusts the teaching of the faith to him alone. He gives up teaching grammar, sells his books of old Greek literature for four obols a day, a few small coins, and sleeps on the ground.

Eusebius says he takes too literally Jesus' saying on those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, and castrates himself. He does it to keep the saying, and to give unbelievers no ground for scandal, since he teaches women as well as men.
lines.note: Too literal is Eusebius's judgment. No other early source used here tells of the deed.

lines.text: Demetrius, learning of it, admires his daring and urges him to keep teaching.

He teaches able pupils geometry, arithmetic and the philosophers, as a help to understanding Scripture. In a letter he says he had to examine what heretics and philosophers taught, as Pantaenus had before him.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.18.2-4 and VI.19.12-13; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 34818-34843, 35259-35268

lines.text: His patron Ambrose pays for more than seven shorthand writers, as many copyists, and girls skilled in fine writing.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.18.1 and VI.23.1-2; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 34778-34816, 35885-35898

lines.text: He learns Hebrew, gets the Hebrew Scriptures from the Jewish people, and searches out Greek translations besides the Seventy, the old Greek translation the churches read. One he finds in a jar at Jericho.
lines.note: Jerome says he learned Hebrew against the habit of his time and people (Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40554-40558).

lines.text: He sets the Hebrew and the Greek translations side by side in columns, the work called the Hexapla.

In a letter to Africanus he explains why. He kept the churches' Greek, so as not to pass a forgery to the churches, and learned the Jewish readings, so as not to quote to Jewish people what their copies lack.
He writes On First Principles at Alexandria, by Eusebius's list of his works.
Porphyry, later a pagan writer against the Christians, meets him when Porphyry is young.
lines.reference: Porphyry, quoted in Eusebius, Church History VI.19.5; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 34984-34991

lines.text: Jerome says he visits Rome when Zephyrinus is bishop there, goes to Antioch at the request of Mammaea, mother of the emperor Alexander, and writes to the emperor Philip and his mother.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40539-40554

timeline.when: Years later; the tenth year of the emperor Alexander
timeline.headline: The break with Demetrius, and the move to Caesarea

lines.text: When war breaks out in Alexandria, he goes to Caesarea, in Palestine. Its bishops ask him to preach and explain Scripture in church, though he is not yet a presbyter, an elder of the church.
Demetrius writes that laymen preaching before bishops has never been heard of. The bishops of Jerusalem and Caesarea answer that holy bishops do ask able men to preach, and name cases.
Demetrius calls him home by letter, and he returns to his work.
Seeing him grow famous, Demetrius writes to bishops everywhere that his castration was most foolish, Eusebius says.
lines.note: Eusebius puts these letters before the ordination; Jerome puts Demetrius's anger after it.

lines.text: Sent to Greece on church business, he passes through Palestine and is ordained presbyter at Caesarea by the bishops there.
lines.note: Jerome says he was going to Athens for the churches of Achaia, with a church letter (Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40532-40538); Photius, summarizing Pamphilus, says he went without his bishop's permission (Library 118; cic/texts/photius_library-v1_freese1920.txt lines 11480-11484).

lines.text: With nothing else to say against him, Demetrius accuses him bitterly over the deed of his youth, and those who ordained him too.
Jerome says the ordination so enraged Demetrius that he wrote everywhere to injure Origen's name.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40532-40538

lines.text: Photius, summarizing Pamphilus, says a gathering of bishops and some presbyters ruled that he must not live or teach in Alexandria, and that Demetrius and some Egyptian bishops later took away his priesthood.
lines.note: A report written about six centuries later, of a lost work; no earlier source used here tells of the gathering.

lines.when: In the tenth year of Alexander
lines.text: He leaves Alexandria for Caesarea, leaving the teaching there to Heraclas.
In his Commentary on John he writes that he came out of the storm and out of Egypt, and that an enemy attacked him in new writings.
lines.reference: Origen, Commentary on John VI.1; cic/texts/anf09_gospel-of-peter-diatessaron-origen-commentaries.xml lines 24727-24740

lines.text: The bishops of Jerusalem and Caesarea attend him as their only teacher and let him explain Scripture in church.

Two brothers, Gregory and Athenodorus, study with him. He finds them keen on Greek and Roman learning, gives them a love of philosophy and turns them to the study of God. After five years both become bishops in Pontus.
Jerome says Gregory, on leaving, gives a speech of thanks to Origen before a large gathering, with Origen present.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 65; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40775-40787

lines.when: When he is over sixty, as they say
lines.text: He lets shorthand writers take down his public talks for the first time, and writes eight books answering Celsus's True Discourse against the Christians.
He writes to Fabian, bishop of Rome, and to many other church leaders about the soundness of his faith.

timeline.when: Under the emperor Decius, and the time of Gallus
timeline.headline: Tortured under Decius, and his death
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, from Origen's own letters

lines.text: Decius persecutes the churches out of hatred for Philip, the emperor before him, Eusebius says.
lines.note: Jerome says Decius was mad against the religion of Philip, whom he had killed (Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40576-40579).

lines.text: For the word of Christ, Origen endures chains, tortures of the body, the iron collar and the dungeon. For many days his feet are stretched four spaces in the stocks, a wooden frame that held a prisoner's feet apart, and he is threatened with fire.
His judge does all he can not to let him die.
He writes letters full of comfort to those who need help.
He dies, aged sixty-nine. Jerome says he died at Tyre and was buried there.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.1; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 39146-39163; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40589-40591
lines.note: Photius says Pamphilus and others wrote that he died a martyr at Caesarea under Decius (Library 118; cic/texts/photius_library-v1_freese1920.txt lines 11449-11454).

lines.text: Pamphilus of Caesarea collects a library of his works and copies most of them by hand.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.32.3; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 36887-36894; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40958-40962

lines.text: Pamphilus, in prison, and Eusebius write a Defense of Origen in six books. Its first book answers from his own words those who said his books, above all On First Principles, differed from the church's teaching.
lines.reference: Photius, Library 118; Pamphilus, Defense of Origen, Book I; cic/texts/photius_library-v1_freese1920.txt lines 11437-11441; cic/texts/pamphilus_apologia-pro-origene-rufinus-lat_lommatzsch1846.txt lines 14630-14706

lines.text: Methodius of Olympus writes On the Resurrection against him, on the body as the soul's fetter.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83; Methodius, in Photius's extracts; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41096-41099; cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 35864-35879

lines.text: Athanasius of Alexandria, defending the Council of Nicaea, calls on him as a witness that the Word always existed with the Father.
lines.reference: Athanasius, On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea 27; cic/texts/npnf204_athanasius-select-works-letters.xml lines 28647-28652

lines.when: In the century after his death
lines.text: Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus get his books and, Socrates says, draw from them the right reading of Scripture and answer the Arians' use of him.
Gregory of Nazianzus sends a friend the Philocalia of Origen, passages chosen from his writings, whose first chapter is on how Scripture is to be read.
lines.reference: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115; Philocalia, chapter I; cic/texts/npnf207_cyril-jerusalem-gregory-nazianzen.xml lines 47445-47451; cic/texts/origen_philocalia_lewis1911.txt lines 44

lines.text: Epiphanius, writing against him, tells that he was made to put incense on an altar fire and was cast out of the church at Alexandria.
lines.note: A hostile account written more than a century after his death.

lines.text: Jerome answers critics of his Latin Old Testament by Origen's marks on the Seventy, and has three of Origen's translations from his library.
lines.reference: Jerome, Preface to Job; Lives of Illustrious Men 54; cic/texts/npnf206_jerome-principal-works.xml lines 47003-47012; cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40562-40564

lines.text: Theophilus of Alexandria writes to the bishops condemning Origen's books, to hide his aim against John Chrysostom, Socrates says.

lines.when: About three centuries after his death
lines.text: A council at Constantinople names him, with his writings, among the heretics in its eleventh anathema.
The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria says Demetrius cut him off for writing books of magic.
lines.reference: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria; cic/texts/severus-al-muqaffa_history-patriarchs-coptic-church-v1_evetts1904.txt lines 10035-10037
